strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation with 17 datasets and 10 seeds each, demonstrating consistent improvements across multiple metrics
Clear motivation for the problem with well-articulated distinction between epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty
Practical innovations like ALEATORIC-R (quantile regression on residuals) improve baseline method stability
Substantial improvements over some baselines (28.2% vs ALEATORIC, 17.4% vs PCS) with thorough ablation studies across three variants
Excellent reproducibility with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and discussion of design choices
Effective case study (Ames Housing) demonstrates adaptive λ selection working as intended
Straightforward algorithm that is easy to implement and apply in practice
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: core contribution is adding one calibration parameter λ; similar ideas exist (UACQR, Bayesian methods) with fixed λ=1 or γ₁=1
Only 3% improvement over strongest single-component baseline (ALEATORIC-R) is modest compared to combinations with PCS
Theoretical guarantees are limited: Lemma 2.1 is informal with k=1 rendering consistency assumption weak; asymptotic result doesn't explain finite-sample behavior
Methodological concerns with data reuse: main algorithm uses Dcal=Dval for both model selection and parameter optimization, risking overfitting of λ without theoretical justification
Parameter selection via very dense grid (4,010 points) on validation data is prone to overfitting; no analysis of grid sensitivity or principled guidance for practitioners
Experimental confounds: three variants use different base models, making it hard to isolate CLEAR's contribution from flexible model selection advantages
UACQR comparison only in variant (c); should appear in all variants for fair assessment of the claimed innovation
Missing computational cost analysis relative to baselines; scalability concerns for large datasets not addressed
Limited scope analysis: when/why does CLEAR help most? No failure case discussion or practitioner guidance on hyperparameter selection

strengths: Addresses practical problem of combining epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty rather than fixing their ratio
Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 17 datasets, 10 seeds, proper train/val/test splits, multiple variants and ablations
Algorithm is clearly presented and easy to understand
Residual-based aleatoric uncertainty (fitting on Yi - f̂(Xi)) is a useful practical insight for stability
Consistent empirical improvements: 17-28% interval width reduction while maintaining nominal coverage
Extensive appendices with detailed results, implementation details, and theoretical discussion
Thorough experiments on synthetic data demonstrating conditional coverage properties
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: essentially combines two existing methods (PCS + CQR) by adding one tunable parameter λ for their ratio. Primarily an engineering contribution, not a conceptual advance
Weak theoretical contribution: Lemma 2.1 is asymptotic and trivial (reduces to known CQR results when epistemic uncertainty vanishes); doesn't match practical algorithm that reuses validation data
Experimental comparisons may be unfair: CLEAR optimizes γ1 and λ (4000+ grid points) on validation data while baselines lack equivalent tuning. Fairest variant (b) relegated to appendix

Theoretical-practice gap: Paper claims asymptotic conditional validity but practical algorithm violates conformal assumptions (reuses D_cal = D_val). Appendix G proposes 'Conformalized CLEAR' but not used by default
Conditional coverage evidence limited to simulations: Real data shows only marginal coverage (PICP≈0.95). Conditional coverage by subgroup not validated on real datasets

Overstated contributions: (1) dual parameters are parameter tuning, not innovation; (2) residual-based quantiles lack direct comparison showing superiority on real data; (3) combining PCS+CQR is straightforward; (4) extending PCS to quantile regression is incremental

Insufficient practical guidance: No sensitivity analysis for λ grid coarseness; case study shows λ ranges 0.6-14.5 across similar settings with no principled selection rule; why quantile loss metric not justified
Structural choice not justified: Form C(x)=f̂(x)±√(γ1·a+γ2·e) is specific; why additive under square root vs multiplicative/max? Not validated against alternatives
Limited scope: Only regression, only α=0.05, only one method combination (PCS+CQR). Classification and other coverage levels deferred
Incomplete evaluation: UACQR baseline relegated to appendix variant (c); no comparison to recent uncertainty disentanglement methods; no analysis of when CLEAR helps most

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 17 datasets with proper methodology (10 seeds each, multiple metrics)
Consistent and substantial practical improvements (28.2% interval width reduction) while maintaining calibration
Well-motivated problem: demonstrates that fixed uncertainty combinations (λ=1 or γ₁=1) are suboptimal and data-dependent
Sound technical execution: proper conformal prediction principles, correct theoretical statements (Lemma 2.1), detailed ablation studies
Useful methodological insights: quantile regression on residuals for aleatoric stability; successful PCS+CQR combination
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, three method variants, extensive appendices with implementation details
Thoughtful case study showing adaptive λ selection across different information regimes
weaknesses: Incremental core innovation: the idea of optimizing two parameters instead of one is straightforward; limited conceptual advance over prior fixed-ratio approaches
Overfitting concerns with two-parameter calibration on validation set insufficiently addressed; paper acknowledges but offers only vague mitigation
Theory-practice gap: asymptotic theory (Lemma 2.1) uses Dcal ≠ Dval, but experiments use Dcal = Dval; Conformalized CLEAR appears more principled but is relegated to appendix
Limited guidance on practical deployment: no clear analysis of when CLEAR outperforms simpler baselines or when to use variants (a), (b), or (c)
Incomplete baseline comparisons: UACQR (conceptually closest method) mostly in appendix; recent methods (EPICSCORE, TabPFN) not empirically evaluated
Missing ablations: decomposition of improvement sources (residual-based aleatoric vs. two-parameter calibration) not provided; sensitivity to λ grid granularity unexplored
Scalability and computational cost not discussed despite requiring ensemble training, multiple data splits, and grid search over ~4000 λ values
Evaluation circularity: quantile loss used for both λ selection and final evaluation; NCIW test-time calibration definition undermines comparison when all methods are calibrated
